# Intestinal lymphangiectasia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the intestine and appendix > Intestinal lymphangiectasia*

[Original Article Link](/library/r90fKR)

---

## Summary

Intestinal lymphangiectasia is a rare disorder characterized by dilatation of intestinal lymphatic vessels, which can lead to <u>protein-losing enteropathy</u>. It may be primary (congenital; also known as Waldmann disease) or secondary to conditions that impair lymphatic flow, such as cardiovascular disorders, <u>neoplasms</u>, or infections. The underlying pathophysiology involves the leakage of <u>chyle</u> into the intestinal lumen, resulting in the loss of <u>proteins</u>, <u>lymphocytes</u>, and lipids. The primary clinical feature is <u>peripheral edema</u>, typically in the lower limbs, which is caused by <u>hypoalbuminemia</u>. Other common manifestations include serous effusions, <u>chronic diarrhea</u>, and fatigue. Diagnosis is confirmed by esophagoduodenoscopy (<u>EGD</u>) and <u>duodenal biopsy</u> findings that show dilated lymphatic vessels. Management is based on dietary modification with a strict low-fat, high-protein diet supplemented with medium-chain <u>triglycerides</u> (MCTs) and <u>fat-soluble vitamins</u>. Pharmacological options such as <u>octreotide</u> or <u>mTOR inhibitors</u> may be considered in rare cases refractory to dietary modification. Surgical or interventional therapies are reserved for focal disease.
